props.title: The Devil's Playground

sections.content: **The Devil's Playground** (1976) marked Fred Schepisi's directorial debut and set a new benchmark for Australian coming-of-age cinema. Set in a Catholic seminary in 1953, it draws from Schepisi's own experiences to craft an unflinching examination of sexual repression and religious dogma. The film shares thematic DNA with **The Thorn Birds** (1983) and **Au Revoir les Enfants** (1987), exploring how institutional religion shapes young minds. Its raw portrayal of adolescent sexuality influenced later works like Doubt (2008) and The Magdalene Sisters (2002).

sections.content: Schepisi's masterful direction creates a claustrophobic atmosphere that mirrors the psychological confinement of its young protagonists. The film's exploration of religious authority echoes through later Australian classics like **Picnic at Hanging Rock** (1975) and **December Boys** (2007). Its unflinching look at Catholic education's impact on sexuality influenced international films like **The Chorus** (2004) and Bad Education (2004).

The film's visual style, with its emphasis on shadowy corridors and austere architecture, established a template for depicting religious institutions that influenced works like **The Name of the Rose** (1986) and **Dead Poets Society** (1989). Cinematographer Ian Baker's naturalistic lighting approach creates an documentary-like authenticity that makes the emotional struggles feel devastatingly real. SUBHEAD: Impact on Religious Cinema

sections.content: **The Devil's Playground** (1976) helped pave the way for more critical examinations of religious institutions in cinema. Its influence can be seen in films like **Calvary** (2014) and **Spotlight** (2015), which similarly tackle complex questions of faith, power, and institutional responsibility. The film's treatment of sexuality within religious contexts influenced later works like **Priest** (1994) and **The Club** (2015).
